Research Corner
Trials • Recruitment • Milestones

A busy month in research: a practical tip from the RELEASE team, a milestone certificate, good news on ABBRUPT funding, and a big number for 2026 so far.

⚠️ RELEASE: How to Calculate the P:F Ratio Thanks for continuing to screen and recruit for RELEASE. We had reason to talk through a patient last week, and I wanted to share advice from Trial HQ. When calculating P:F ratios, please use the standard, non-temperature-corrected PaO₂ reported by the blood gas analyser.

Why? The usual PaO₂/FiO₂ thresholds for ARDS classification and trial eligibility are based on PaO₂ measured by the analyser at 37°C. The temperature-corrected value is a calculated estimate adjusted to the patient's actual body temperature, not a separate direct measurement. Using it can introduce temperature-dependent variation and, as we have seen, may move a patient across an eligibility threshold. For consistency across patients and sites, the standard PaO₂ is the right value to use.

Recruitment: Where We Are

By the end of August we had successfully enrolled 100 patients into research on Critical Care since January. That is a great achievement, and it hopefully sets us up to beat last year's total of 119. In August itself, 24 patients were screened and 6 were recruited. Thank you to everyone who keeps screening.

Clinical Updates
Protocols • Guidelines • Equipment

Several practice points this month, with a few things to look out for at the bedside. The bigger guidance documents are linked so you can read the full detail.

🧪 Renal Replacement Therapy: Consistent Fluid Balance Terms Consistency in how fluid management is described for patients on renal replacement therapy is essential so that clinical plans are understood and carried out correctly and safely. Until now, different terms have been used for the same plan, and some have been read differently between team members. From now on, the terms below are used by all team members.

At initial set-up, if no endpoints have been described by the medical team, set up for zero balance. Because of the Unity set-up, fluid targets are described overall in 12-hour blocks: 0000 - 1200h and 1200 - 0000h.
Judged over 12-hour blocks: 0000 - 1200h and 1200 - 0000h
Cycling
No net change from the machine
Fluid is neither added nor removed by the machine. The 12h balance comes from other sources only.
Balance = other in / out
Zero balance
End of 12h: 0 mL
Take fluid off if intake is building up, or give fluid if losses exceed intake.
Default at initial set-up if no endpoint is stated
Negative
End of 12h: -XXX mL
Overall value set by the medical team. Adjust the machine to account for intake and output.
Value stated by the medical team
Positive
End of 12h: +XXX mL
Overall value set by the medical team. Adjust the machine and IV fluid rate.
Value stated by the medical team
  • Cycling: fluid is neither added nor removed by the dialysis machine. The 12h balance depends on intake and output from other sources.
  • Zero balance: at the end of the 12h block the overall calculated balance is zero. Fluid may need to be taken off by the machine if input (including drugs, feed and other fluids) is building up against losses, or given if losses such as diarrhoea or drains exceed the total intake.
  • Negative balance: at the end of the 12h block the overall balance is -XXX mL, as stated by the medical team. It is an overall value, so the machine setting must be adjusted to account for intake and output.
  • Positive balance: at the end of the 12h block the overall balance is +XXX mL, as stated by the medical team. The machine setting and the rate of IV fluid will need adjusting to account for intake and output.
⚓ AnchorFast: Now Our Standard ETT Securement Thanks to Neelam for this one. AnchorFast is now our standard method of securing the ETT and should be used for the majority of intubated patients. If your patient doesn't have one, check why, and get one on unless there is a genuine clinical reason not to. Facial hair alone is not a reason to exclude a patient; where appropriate, discuss shaving to allow safe application.

Once it is on, keep the tube moving: reposition the ETT regularly, check the surrounding skin, and use the ventilator arm to support the circuit. AnchorFast can stay in place for up to 7 days if it is secure and intact. They are kept in the store room, in a labelled drawer.

For patient selection, contraindications, application and ongoing care, see the AnchorFast Clinical Guideline / SOP: MyDoc reference number 3493. It is also on Connect and on SPARC. Paper copies are in zones 1 and 3.

🫡 Patients with a Tracheostomy: Weaning Support Following earlier communications about avoiding SmartCare in patients who have had a tracheostomy, please note that the extubation checklist criteria of pressure support 5 cmH₂O and PEEP 5 cmH₂O are also not intended for this patient group.

Tracheostomy insertion should not automatically prompt an immediate drop in respiratory support to these levels. Patients who need ventilatory weaning should have a structured, graduated reduction in support, started at the appropriate time, which may not be immediately after insertion. Rapid reduction can be counter-productive, get in the way of taking part in rehabilitation, and delay weaning and recovery. Weaning can be achieved from a range of modes and support levels, including VC-SIMV where appropriate. The key principle is to keep enough respiratory support to give rest between tracheostomy mask sprints and physical rehabilitation sessions.

An exception may be patients who had a tracheostomy mainly for neurological assessment or airway access, where respiratory function and deconditioning are not the main concerns. Questions or individual cases: please talk to Nicki or Ahmed.

📋 Did You Know? NSE and Prognosis An NSE above 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h after ROSC is one of the recognised markers of a poor outcome after cardiac arrest. The 2025 ERC / ESICM guidance uses it as part of a multimodal assessment - it counts alongside other findings such as pupillary and corneal reflexes, SSEPs, EEG and imaging, and is not used on its own.
🩹 Donor Optimisation Bundle Is Live The donor optimisation bundle for patients proceeding to organ donation after death by neurological criteria is now live. Activate it by entering "brain stem death" in diagnosis / problems. Please see your emails for guidance, and contact Dr Kieran Donnelly or Dean Farrington the first time you use it.
👁️ Pupillometer: Use It for the Right Patients Dean tells us the unit has used 360 SmartGuard covers for the pupillometers over the last 12 months. Please make sure the SOP criteria are followed. Use it for:
  • Patients with pupillary changes on initial neurological assessment
  • All patients with a suspected acquired brain injury awaiting a CT scan
  • All patients with a diagnosed acquired brain injury on CT
  • Patients on the perceived devastating brain injury pathway
Do not use the pupillometer for general neurological assessment in patients without an acquired brain injury - use a pen torch.
📝 Updated Nursing Care Plans Coming Soon Nursing care plans have traditionally been one plan for each of the nine care elements - the real-time recipe for nursing care delivery. The CCS care plans needed updating, and the brief was a simpler, more user-friendly version on Unity as a bedside reference. Referenced nursing care plans will sit in a care plan library on MyDoc (or SPARC), and all plans will be reviewed within the audit cycle. Happy care planning! (Thanks to Sarah Gould.)

Safety & Quality
Patient Safety • Governance • Audit
⚖️ Duty of Candour: Act - Record - Communicate A reminder that Duty of Candour applies when a patient safety incident results in moderate to severe harm, including psychological harm, or death. The lead clinician - the most senior professional responsible for the patient's care in the specialty where the incident occurred - holds overall responsibility for completing the requirements and documentation. Keep the incident record updated at every stage.
  1. Speak & record - immediately / ASAP. Give a verbal apology. Record the date, time and details of the discussion on Safeguard.
  2. Confirm in writing - within 10 working days. Attach the initial letter or written confirmation to the incident and update the date after harm is confirmed.
  3. Share the final outcome - within 10 working days. After the investigation is complete, attach the final letter or report to the incident and update the date.

Before sending any letter: liaise with the Patient Safety Team first, then contact the patient, family or next of kin to ask whether they wish to receive the investigation outcome. Duty of Candour is complete only when the final letter or report has been sent. Need advice? swbh.patientsafety@nhs.net

📞 Reaching the SHOs and Registrar The SHOs and Registrar can be contacted at any time through the bleep system if you need them and their baton phones are not working or out of range (some areas of the Trust have poor coverage). In an emergency, you can also dial 2222 and ask switch to fast-bleep them to attend your location.

🔍 New Glidescopes on ICU We have begun using our brand new Glidescopes on ICU, one in each zone, with a go-live date of 23 September. Please take a moment to familiarise yourself with the connections that are compatible with the blades on the packaging - they are different from theatres. A rigid stylet is also recommended with any hyperangulated blade; please take care on insertion to avoid trauma.

There will be future pop-in refresher sessions from the Verathon team for anyone who wants a more formal update. In the meantime we will stop using the CMACs as we finish the last blades in stock. Questions about use can go to Dr Wasim Mir. Special thanks to Jenny Noble and Rebecca O'Dwyer, who helped with purchasing and ordering. Happy intubating!
Check the connection on the blade packaging before you use it. It is not the same as in theatres.
Another view of the blade connection and monitor cable.
Hyperangle blade with a stylet. Use a rigid stylet with any hyperangulated blade.
